Variants.Content: Gongyangmen is a pass point in the northern road system. Northern place names are often taken directly from mountains, animals, rocks or local legends; the focus of Gongyang Gate is not on the magnificence of the name, but on the "gate" - it closes the vast wilderness into a passage that can be guarded, taxed, inspected or closed. The north does not have as many bridges and towns as the south. A passable mountain pass, ferry or causeway is often enough to change the route of marching and business travel. Gatekeepers need food, water, firewood, horns and judgment of the weather. Stone walls alone are not enough.

Entry Ramsgate Local families also rely on firewood, hunting grounds, peat, salt fish, and granaries to survive the long winter; if any road, well, spring, or wharf fails, the price will fall on them first.

Entry Ramsgate They also recognize the accents, laws, and credentials of the North; reputations can travel great distances from taverns, but true distances must still be measured by wheel, oar, or horse's hoof.

Entry Ramsgate If you can supply supplies, avoid danger, and find a guide, it is worth marking in your itinerary; if you don't have these three things, no matter how loud your family name is, it won't be able to save the lost.

The craftsmen used their hands to measure the quarried stones, logging, iron parts, goat hair, and wall foundations built close to the mountain. The priests used rituals to continue the burials left by the old gods, weirwood trees, and ancestors. A stronghold was therefore not just a lord's hall, but also a place where weddings and funerals, vows, labor and local memories recurred.

Entry Ramsgate They care about firewood, hunting grounds, peat, salt fish, and granaries that can survive the long winter. They also care about whether seeds are left after the grain collection and whether the city gates are open in times of disaster. When people from afar see coats of arms, they see whether there will be food to eat tomorrow.
